After losing both parents, his sight and the support of relatives, Chinedu Nkwocha, popularly known as Loka Lawya, found hope in the kindness of strangers and a Catholic nun. Now a University of Port Harcourt student, comedian and musician, he tells CHIJIOKE IREMEKA how he overcame abandonment and is seeking opportunities to fulfil his entertainment dreams Could you tell us about your family background? My name is Chinedu Nkwocha, popularly known as Loka Lawya. I am an orphan, a visually impaired comedian, musician and content creator. I own Loka Lawya Entertainment Venture. I was born on April 1, 2000, in Ajegunle, Lagos, and I am currently a 100-level Broadcasting student at the University of Port Harcourt. I hail from Owerri North Local Government Area of Imo State but was born and raised in Ajegunle, Lagos. I am the second of my father’s four sons. My father had three wives. I was born into an average family, but the death of my parents changed everything about my life. At what point did you become visually impaired? I became an orphan at the age of 12 and completely blind at 14. My eyes started having problems before my mother died in 2009. After her death, my father was the only person who could take me to the General Hospital, Ikeja, for treatment. According to the eye specialist, I had cataracts. At some point, I was scheduled for surgery in 2011, but I never made it to the hospital. A few days before the scheduled date, my father died. I was told that he died from a cold. After his death, everything about my life changed. As an orphan, I had nobody to help me or take me to the hospital. There was no money, parental support or anyone to sponsor my treatment. Consequently, I became completely blind in 2012. Perhaps I would not have lost my sight if my father had not died when he did. What about your siblings and other family members? My father’s death marked the end of the relatively comfortable life I had known. He was a hardworking man who did different jobs to provide for us and make us happy. At one point, he worked in a shipping company involved in clearing and forwarding at Apapa. When things became difficult, he took up commercial motorcycling to ensure we had food to eat. He had three wives and four sons, and I am the second child. After his death, I went to live with my aunt in Ajegunle, Lagos. Her husband also had two wives, and she was the younger wife. Initially, they tried to accommodate me, but the first wife eventually started complaining. Consequently, they took me back to my father’s house in Surulere, where I experienced terrible maltreatment. That was where I encountered real hardship. My father had three wives, and my mother had died long before then. You said you experienced terrible hardship. What exactly happened? In Surulere, I nearly drowned in a flood. My father’s family did not accept me, and I still do not know why. I was not allowed to sleep inside the room. Since it was a face-me-I-face-you apartment, I slept on a borrowed bench in the corridor every night, with my belongings kept outside. One particular night remains fresh in my memory. I was sleeping on the bench when heavy rain fell and floodwater covered me. I was partially sighted at the time, an orphan left outside in the rain. It was only by God’s grace that I was not swept away or drowned. Sometimes, I went without food, but God used two people to keep me alive: my grandfather, Dennis Nkwocha, a pensioner, and a man called Mr Monday. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. Add us to your Preferred Sources My grandfather loved me dearly and fed me from his pension. Even when his children complained about the money he spent on me, he continued to care for me. He would buy bread and make tea for me, and that was sometimes all I had to eat for the day. Mr Monday also had a restaurant in the same compound. Because I was partially sighted, I helped him peel seasoning cubes, wash plates and serve customers. In the afternoon, he would give me eba and soup. Those are experiences I will never forget. My own relatives rejected me, but God used other people to give me hope. You are now a Broadcasting student at the University of Port Harcourt. How did your educational journey begin as an orphan? While living in Surulere, I met a Catholic friend named Ebuka, who used to clean Pacelli School for the Blind and Partially Sighted Children every Saturday. One day, he invited me to accompany him, and I agreed. That was where I met Reverend Sister Jane Onyeneri, who was the school’s principal in 2014. She took pity on me and asked about my sight. After listening to my story, she asked me to invite my relatives to register me at the school for free. However, none of them was willing to do so, claiming they were too busy. Eventually, Chikaodi, the relative who had treated me particularly badly, took me to the school. On arrival, Sister Jane asked him whether he wanted to take me back home or leave me there so the school could assume full responsibility for my care. My relatives made it clear that they did not want me back. Since then, the Reverend Sisters of the Handmaids of the Holy Child Jesus, through Sister Jane Onyeneri and the Catholic Church, have taken responsibility for my welfare and education. In 2022, I was handed over to another HHCJ Reverend Sister, Agnes Onwudiwe, who has continued to care for me. What was your experience like at Pacelli School and King’s College, Lagos? Before getting into Pacelli, I thought my life had ended. I wondered how a blind orphan like me could ever go to school. But Pacelli restored my hope. If not for that Saturday when I accompanied Ebuka, who was cleaning the school, and met Sister Jane, who took pity on me, I might have remained in Surulere, enduring maltreatment. You mentioned that you are a comedian. Is that your ambition? My ambition is to become a professional broadcaster, a renowned comedian and a musician. How did you become a comedian? I started at Pacelli School for the Blind. After regaining hope in 2013/2014, I began organising and hosting social nights at the school. That was where my journey into comedy and music began. I started performing as an underground entertainer in 2015, and that was how Loka Lawya Entertainment Venture was born. What challenges do you face as a comedian living with visual impairment? There are many challenges. I cannot see the camera properly or clearly observe my audience’s reactions. I also lack a good phone and adequate lighting to create content. In music, I released a secular song titled Dance in 2023, although I am yet to venture into gospel music. However, recording a single song now costs me N50,000, even after the discount my friend gives me when I plead with him. That amount covers only the recording, excluding promotion and advertising. Music production is expensive, and because I cannot afford the costs, I had to put music on hold and concentrate on comedy. How do you get comedy engagements? Through friends and by performing at small events in Ajegunle and Surulere. I also still host events at Pacelli School. I do not have a manager or sponsor. Do you think Nigeria and Nigerians treat persons with disabilities fairly? No. There is a lot of stigmatisation. Many people think that anyone who cannot see is useless. Do persons with disabilities have equal opportunities to thrive in Nigeria? No, we do not have equal opportunities. What appeal would you make to stakeholders in Nigeria’s entertainment industry and Nigerians generally? I am appealing to established comedians, musicians, broadcasters and other stakeholders in the Nigerian entertainment industry to remember Loka Lawya: the boy who slept in a passage at No. 52, Ashimowu Bakare Street, Surulere; the boy who endured the rain while sleeping on a bench and was rejected by his relatives but accepted by Reverend Sister Jane Onyeneri. I do not want pity; I want an opportunity and sponsorship for my Loka Lawya Entertainment Venture. Their support would go a long way towards helping me achieve my dreams. What is your advice to others facing similar challenges? Do not give up. I was born into an average family. I lost my mother in 2009 and my father in 2011. Before his death, my father rode a commercial motorcycle to provide for us. I lost my sight in 2012, slept in a passage in Surulere while my belongings were kept outside, and was rejected by my relatives. But God used people such as my grandfather, Nkwocha, who bought bread for me with his pension; Mr Monday, who gave me eba; my friend Ebuka, who took me to Pacelli School while cleaning there on Saturdays; and Reverend Sister Jane Onyeneri, who took pity on me, to give me a future. If I could move from sleeping on a bench in the rain to studying at the University of Port Harcourt, then others facing challenges can also overcome them and achieve their dreams.
